Link
Cutting compute costs by 30% by redesigning AI responses around common tasks
AI Product design
Role: lead product designer
Team: product manager, data scientist, 2 engineers, policy consultant
Summary
Context
A new partnership would bring 100+ users we couldn't afford to support at current compute costs
Approach
Users were expensive because answers didn't fit their task, so they kept asking follow-ups
Outcome
Compute cost per task fell [30%], and we supported the partnership within budget
A partnership bringing 100+ new users would have pushed compute costs over budget
I worked with our engineering team to lower costs without making the product worse
Making each answer less detailed was cheaper but would have backfired because
thinner answers drive more follow-ups
If answers got thinner, we'd lose the savings in volume while degrading the experience. Before cutting anything, I wanted to understand why users sent so many messages.
2/3 of messages came from 3 tasks where users had to piece text answers together themselves
With our data scientist, I analyzed 90 chat sessions and tagged each by what the user was trying to accomplish.
Task 1
Mapping stakeholders
Who is involved and how they connect
Who are the key funders in this area who I may be able to get funding from?
Who are the stakeholders whose goals I need to keep in mind when designing this new policy?
How do I get in touch with these stakeholders?
Task 3
Reviewing past policies
What has been tried and when
What was done in the past to address this issue?
What can we learn from these past initiatives?
What was missing from these past initiatives that requires new solutions?
Task 2
Understanding current policies
What is active now and how it overlaps
What current solutions exist?
How much funding was received by projects in this space recently?
What are the current projects missing that requires a new solution?
In 12 user interviews I led, users described asking follow-ups to retrieve dates, reformat lists, or find which policies overlapped
The answers had the information but not the shape they needed
Sample: Getting the data to the correct “shape” took 4 turns
Show me policy timeline for youth unemployment in Kenya
Can you list them in order by year?
Which of these were running at the same time from 2023 and 2024?
Which ones are still active as of 2026?
Visual answers cost more per message but less per task because one visual replaced on average 2-4 follow-ups
Measured per message, visual answers looked like the wrong direction. Measured per completed task, they were cheaper.
Users also told us visuals were easier to skim and made patterns visible faster. Some said visuals were a reason to choose PolicyCopilot over a general-purpose AI tool.
Showing high-value visuals by default and offering costly ones on request kept spending in check
With an engineer, I plotted each candidate content type by user value and expected compute cost:
High cost
High user value
Low cost
Low user value
Venn diagram
Best for: stakeholders
Flowchart
Best for: stakeholders
Euclidian graph
Best for: stakeholders
Bubble chart
Best for: current and past policies
Scatter plot
Best for: current and past policies
Gantt chart
Best for: current and past policies
These visuals were selected as the ones to build
Each visual answered questions users previously needed several follow-ups to answer
“Show me policy timeline for youth unemployment in Kenya”
Before
Text lists forced users to rebuild the timeline in their heads
Show me policy timeline for youth unemployment in Kenya
Can you list them in order by year?
Which of these were running at the same time from 2023 and 2024?
Which ones are still active as of 2026?
After
The Gantt chart makes order and overlap visible immediately
“What policies have impacted conservation in West Africa from 2016 onwards?”
Before
Text responses did not reveal patterns and required a new followup question to obtain new information
What policies have impacted conservation in West Africa from 2016 onwards?
How much funding was obtained by each of the initiatives
Are there any patterns with what gets funded
After
Sizing bubbles by funding received showed which projects attract funders without users comparing figures
Cost per task dropped 30% while task completion held steady, so we could onboard all 100+ partnership users
Stats
change in compute cost per task
average messages per task
cost per message (accepted trade-off)
The cheapest AI answer is the one that finishes the task in the fewest turns

If I did this again, I'd measure task success from the beginning rather than relying on message count, since fewer messages can also mean users gave up. Next, I'd explore extending the approach to other task types.

I want to look into youth unemployment in Pakistan. I've been reading that the actual official youth unemployment rate is pretty low but that the number might be misleading and that the real issue is underemployment or perhaps greater reliance on informal work (not joblessness).
Summary

The tension between a low official youth unemployment rate and concern about underemployment or informal work is the core puzzle here; the framing needs to avoid treating joblessness as the only labour-market problem. I have a few more questions so I can better understand the problem:
